sourcingNote:
This section goes further than the other culture topics: it is also about how people in Portugal live, talk and behave, not only about rules.
So it has its own rule. A statement about people either rests on a statistic or an official source, or it is marked as common practice. Under a topic you find the sources and the date they are from. Where a topic has no source list, it describes common practice: it is not a survey result, and it varies by person, age and region. We write "many" or "most", never "the Portuguese are ...". About 10.7 million people live in Portugal (INE estimate), and they are all different: young and old, from Minho to the Algarve, from Madeira and the Azores, from big cities and from villages, born in Portugal or abroad.
Where something is debated, both sides are shown. Rules and figures change; if in doubt, the linked official source is right.

topics.title: Saying hello: dois beijinhos, handshake, Bom dia
topics.intro: In Portugal, people usually greet each other with words first, and friends and acquaintances often give dois beijinhos (two light kisses on the cheeks). At work, a handshake is normal when you meet someone for the first time. Many people also say “Bom dia” to neighbours on the stairs and to staff when they enter a shop or a café.
topics.question: Como é que se cumprimenta no teu país? (How do people greet each other in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

Dois beijinhos: one light kiss on each cheek, often just cheek to cheek. It is common between two women and between a woman and a man who know each other, and in families. Men usually shake hands; close male friends and relatives may hug.
The greeting follows the time of day: “Bom dia” until lunch, “Boa tarde” in the afternoon, “Boa noite” in the evening and at night. “Olá” is informal and fits any time.
At a first meeting people often say “Muito prazer” or just “Prazer”. With colleagues you see every day, “Bom dia” or “Olá, tudo bem?” is enough.
“Com licença” (excuse me) is said when you enter an office or a room, or when you pass someone. When you leave a shop, many people say “Obrigado, bom dia” or “Até logo”.
topics.context: If you are not sure, wait for the other person. If they lean in for dois beijinhos, do the same. If they put out a hand, shake it. Nobody will mind a small mistake, and a clear “Bom dia” is never wrong.
phrases: Bom dia! (Good morning! Until lunch.)
Olá, tudo bem? (Hi, how are things?)
Tudo bem, obrigado. E contigo? (Fine, thanks. And you?)
Muito prazer. (Nice to meet you.)
Com licença. (Excuse me. When you come in or pass.)
Até logo! (See you later!)

quiz.prompt: You meet your new boss for the first time. What do most people do?
quiz.explain: A handshake is normal at a first meeting at work. Dois beijinhos come later, or between people who already know each other.

quiz.prompt: It is 4 pm and you enter a small shop. Which greeting fits?
quiz.explain: “Boa tarde” is for the afternoon. “Bom dia” is used until lunch, “Boa noite” in the evening.

quiz.prompt: You walk into an office where people are working. What do you say?
quiz.explain: “Com licença” is the polite way to come in or pass. “Até logo” is for leaving, “De nada” answers a thank you.

topics.title: Queues and personal space
topics.intro: In Portugal, many offices, health centres and supermarket counters give you a senha, a numbered ticket, and you wait until your number appears. Where there is no machine, you ask who is last. Many people also stand quite close and touch an arm when they talk.
topics.question: Como é que se espera a vez no teu país? (How do people wait their turn in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the place and the situation.

Senhas are everywhere: at the Loja do Cidadão, at Finanças, at the centro de saúde, at the post office and at the meat or cheese counter in many supermarkets. Take a ticket first, then watch the screen for your number and your counter.
Where there is no ticket machine, for example at a small market stall, ask “Quem é o último?” (Who is last?). Someone answers “Sou eu”, and you go after that person.

Many counters have atendimento prioritário (priority service), for example for pregnant women, older people, people with a disability and people with a small child on their lap. Others are expected to let them go first.
If you touch someone by accident, say “Desculpe”. To get past, say “Com licença”.
topics.context: At an office, check that you took the right senha: there are often different letters for different services, such as A for one matter and B for another. If you are not sure, ask at the reception: “Para isto, qual é a senha?”
phrases: Quem é o último? (Who is last?)
Sou eu. (It's me. Said by the last person.)
Com licença, posso passar? (Excuse me, can I get past?)
Desculpe. (Sorry.)
Já tirou senha? (Have you taken a ticket?)
Eu estava primeiro. (I was here first.)

quiz.prompt: You arrive at a market stall with no clear line. What do you ask?
quiz.explain: You ask who is last, and then you know when it is your turn.

quiz.prompt: At the Loja do Cidadão, what do you usually do first?
quiz.explain: Most offices work with senhas. Your number appears on a screen with the counter.

quiz.prompt: You bump into someone by accident. What do you say?
quiz.explain: “Desculpe” is the normal word for a small mistake.

topics.title: Please and thank you
topics.intro: In Portugal, many requests are softened: people say “Queria um café” (I would like a coffee) rather than “Quero”, and they call a waiter with “Se faz favor”. “Obrigado” and “Obrigada” are said often, and the form follows the person who speaks. Learn a few of these small words and you will sound polite and natural.
topics.question: Como é que se pede alguma coisa no teu país? (How do people ask for things in your country?)

table.label: What you say, and what it does
rows: Queria um café, por favor.
A polite order. The past form queria (I wanted) softens the request.
Se faz favor!
Calls a waiter or a shop assistant. It also means please at the end of a sentence.
Obrigado. / Obrigada.
Thank you. A man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada, whoever they are talking to.
Desculpe. / Peço desculpa.
Sorry, or excuse me to get attention. Peço desculpa is a little more formal.
Com licença.
Excuse me, I am coming in or passing.
De nada. / Não tem de quê.
You are welcome, as an answer to a thank you.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age and the situation.
Requests are often made in the imperfect or as a question: “Queria…”, “Podia…?”, “Pode dizer-me…?”. A bare “Quero” can sound abrupt to some people, especially from an adult stranger.
“Obrigado” agrees with the speaker, not with the listener: a woman says “obrigada” to everybody, a man says “obrigado” to everybody.
With older people and in offices, many people use o senhor or a senhora with the verb instead of tu: “O senhor pode ajudar-me?”
Requests are often indirect. “Não sei se seria possível…” (I don't know if it would be possible…) is a common, polite way to ask for something difficult.
topics.context: If someone sounds short, it is usually not anger: listen to the tone and the greeting. A “Bom dia” at the start and an “obrigado” or “obrigada” at the end make any request warm.
phrases: Queria uma bica, se faz favor. (An espresso, please.)
Se faz favor! (Excuse me! To call the waiter.)
Desculpe, pode ajudar-me? (Excuse me, can you help me?)
Muito obrigada, bom dia! (Thank you very much, have a good day! Said by a woman.)
Não tem de quê. (You're welcome.)
Peço desculpa pelo atraso. (I apologise for being late.)

quiz.prompt: A woman thanks a male waiter. What does she say?
quiz.explain: The form follows the speaker: a woman says obrigada, whoever she is talking to.

quiz.prompt: In a café you want to call the waiter. What do many people say?
quiz.explain: “Se faz favor” calls a waiter. “Com licença” is for coming in or passing.

quiz.prompt: Why do many people say “Queria um café” and not “Quero um café”?
options: Because queria sounds softer and more polite
Because quero is a Brazilian word
quiz.answer: Because queria sounds softer and more polite
quiz.explain: The imperfect queria is a common way to soften a request. Quero is correct Portuguese, just more direct.

topics.title: Time and timing
topics.intro: In Portugal, lunch is an important break, and many people eat between half past twelve and two. Among friends, a little lateness is common, but at work, at the doctor and at an appointment people expect you on time. Some small words, such as “já vou” and “logo”, are less exact than they sound.
topics.question: O que acontece no teu país se chegares atrasado? (What happens in your country if you arrive late?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the region, the age and the situation.
Many people have lunch (o almoço) between about 12:30 and 14:00 and dinner (o jantar) between about 20:00 and 21:30. Some small shops and offices in smaller towns close for lunch.
Among friends, 10 or 15 minutes late is often normal. If you are later, send a message: “Chego daqui a dez minutos”.
At work, in a job interview and at an appointment (at AIMA, Finanças or the centro de saúde), be on time. A booked time is a fixed time, and you may lose your turn if you are late.
“Já vou” means “I'm coming”, but not always this second. “Logo” means later (today), not “soon”: “Até logo” is see you later. “Logo se vê” means we'll see. If it matters, ask for a day and an hour.
topics.context: If you will be late, say so early and give a short reason. A short message is better than silence.
phrases: A que horas combinamos? (What time shall we meet?)
Chego daqui a dez minutos. (I'll be there in ten minutes.)
Desculpa o atraso. (Sorry I'm late. Informal.)
Já vou! (I'm coming!)
Amanhã a que horas, exatamente? (Tomorrow at what time, exactly?)
Tenho consulta às dez. (I have an appointment at ten.)

quiz.prompt: You have an appointment at the centro de saúde at ten. When do you arrive?
options: At ten, or a bit before
quiz.answer: At ten, or a bit before
quiz.explain: At appointments and at work, people expect you on time.

quiz.prompt: A friend says “Até logo.” What does it mean?
quiz.explain: In Portugal logo means later. It is not an exact time.

quiz.prompt: When do many people have lunch?
quiz.explain: Lunch is usually between about half past twelve and two, and it is often a proper meal.

topics.title: Paying the bill
topics.intro: In Portugal, friends often take turns to pay, or they split the bill: pagar a meias (half each) or each person paying their own. Many people send their share by MB WAY, a phone app linked to Portuguese bank cards. And at the till you will often hear one question: “Com contribuinte?”
topics.question: Quem paga no teu país quando se sai em grupo? (Who pays in your country when people go out together?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.
“Hoje pago eu” or “Fica por minha conta” means I am paying today. Next time someone else pays: “Agora é a minha vez”.
“Pagar a meias” means paying half each. In a group, people often divide the bill equally, or each person pays what they had: “Cada um paga o seu”.
MB WAY is a payment app linked to Portuguese bank cards. You can send money to a phone number, so many people use it to pay their share of a bill.

At the till you are often asked “Com contribuinte?” or “Quer fatura com NIF?”. If you give your NIF (tax number), the receipt is registered with the tax office, which can count for your annual tax return. You can also say “Sem contribuinte, obrigado”.
topics.context: Offering to pay once is normal; if the other person insists, accept and thank them. If you prefer to pay your part, say it early and kindly: “Eu pago o meu, está bem?”
phrases: A conta, se faz favor. (The bill, please.)
Hoje pago eu. (I'm paying today.)
Pagamos a meias? (Shall we go halves?)
Mando-te por MB WAY. (I'll send it to you by MB WAY.)
Com contribuinte, se faz favor. (With my tax number, please.)
Cada um paga o seu. (Everyone pays their own.)

quiz.prompt: A friend says “Hoje pago eu.” What does that mean?
quiz.explain: Next time, it is often the other person's turn.

quiz.prompt: The cashier asks “Com contribuinte?” What does she want to know?
options: If you want your tax number (NIF) on the receipt
quiz.answer: If you want your tax number (NIF) on the receipt
quiz.explain: With your NIF, the receipt is registered with the tax office. You can also say no.

quiz.prompt: What is MB WAY?
options: A phone app for sending money
quiz.answer: A phone app for sending money
quiz.explain: MB WAY is linked to Portuguese bank cards and sends money to a phone number.

topics.title: Small talk and the café
topics.intro: In Portugal, much small talk happens at the café da esquina, the café on the corner, where regulars have their coffee standing at the counter. Another place is the stairs of your building: a short conversa de escada with a neighbour. Easy topics are the weather, food, football and the place you live.
topics.question: Sobre o que é que se fala com pessoas novas no teu país? (What do people talk about with new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.
Many people go to the same café every day. After a while the staff may ask “O costume?” (The usual?). It is an easy place to say a few words and be recognised.
A conversa de escada is the short chat with a neighbour on the stairs or in the lift: the weather, the noise, the building. It is a normal way to get to know the people you live with.

Safe topics for a first talk: food, where you are from, the weather, the town, travel and work. Football is a big topic, but many people support Benfica, FC Porto or Sporting with passion, so ask before you joke.
Many people avoid strong opinions about politics, religion or money with people they do not know well. Questions about salary are usually too personal at first.
topics.context: People may ask questions that feel personal, for example if you are married or have children. Usually it is interest, not a test. You can answer briefly or say “Prefiro não falar disso”.
phrases: Então, tudo bem? (So, how are things?)
De onde é? (Where are you from? Formal.)
Vamos tomar um café? (Shall we have a coffee?)
Hoje está um calor! (It's so hot today!)
Estou em Portugal há um ano. (I've been in Portugal for a year.)
És do Benfica ou do Porto? (Do you support Benfica or Porto?)

quiz.prompt: The waiter at your café asks “O costume?” What does he mean?
quiz.explain: O costume is the usual. Regulars often get the same order every day.

quiz.prompt: Which topic is usually safe for a first talk?
quiz.explain: Food, the weather and the town are easy topics. Salary and politics are more personal.

quiz.prompt: What is a conversa de escada?
options: A meeting of the owners of a building
A short chat with a neighbour on the stairs
A phone call to the landlord
quiz.answer: A short chat with a neighbour on the stairs
quiz.explain: Escada means stairs. It is the small talk you have with neighbours in the building.

topics.title: Making friends
topics.intro: In Portugal, friendships often start in small groups: the building, the neighbourhood, an association, a sports club, a class or the school gate. Many people first meet in a WhatsApp group and only later in person. It takes time, but small steps help.
topics.question: Onde é que se conhece gente nova no teu país? (Where do people meet new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the city, the age and the person.
Many buildings have a WhatsApp group for the condomínio. It is used for repairs, noise, deliveries and small problems. Say hello when you join, and keep messages short.

The condomínio is the group of owners in a building. They hold an assembleia de condóminos (owners' meeting) about costs and repairs. Tenants usually do not vote, but they can ask the landlord or the building manager.
Associações and coletividades (local clubs) run sport, music, dance and festivals in many towns. Joining one, or volunteering, is a common way to meet people.
Language exchanges are popular in the big cities. At school, parents often have a WhatsApp group for each class.
topics.context: “Temos de combinar qualquer coisa” (We must arrange something) is often a friendly wish rather than a plan. Suggest a day: “E se fosse no sábado?” A concrete offer helps a friendship start.
phrases: Sou o vizinho do terceiro esquerdo. (I'm the neighbour from the third floor, left.)
Há algum grupo de WhatsApp do prédio? (Is there a WhatsApp group for the building?)
Querem ir beber um café? (Do you all want to go for a coffee?)
E se fosse no sábado? (How about Saturday?)
Procuro um intercâmbio de línguas. (I'm looking for a language exchange.)
Posso inscrever-me na associação? (Can I join the association?)

quiz.prompt: What is the condomínio?
options: The group of owners in a building
quiz.answer: The group of owners in a building
quiz.explain: The owners decide about costs and repairs at the assembleia de condóminos.

quiz.prompt: A new acquaintance says “Temos de combinar qualquer coisa.” What helps make it real?
quiz.explain: The phrase is often a friendly wish. A concrete day, for example “E se fosse no sábado?”, turns it into a plan.

quiz.prompt: Where can you meet people with the same hobby?
quiz.explain: Local associations and clubs run sport, music and festivals in many towns.

topics.title: How hiring works
topics.intro: In Portugal, employers look at your currículo, and personal contacts also matter. Job portals, recruitment agencies, the public employment service IEFP and word of mouth all play a part. Many new contracts start with a trial period, the período experimental.
topics.question: Como é que se procura trabalho no teu país? (How do people look for work in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the sector, the company, the region and the age of the applicant.
A photo on the CV is common but not required. Many people use the Europass format. Ask someone in your field what is usual.
Job portals, LinkedIn and recruitment agencies are widely used. The IEFP (Instituto do Emprego e Formação Profissional) has job centres (centros de emprego) and an online job board.
Personal contacts count. Getting a job only through a connection is called a “cunha”, a word usually used critically. Asking people you know for tips is normal.

Many contracts begin with a período experimental (trial period), during which either side can end the contract more easily. Its length depends on the type of contract and the job; read your contract and ask.

pros: A personal recommendation can open a door quickly.
A clear one- or two-page CV is easy to read and compare.
Smaller companies often decide fast, after one conversation.
cons: People without a network in Portugal can feel left out.
A photo, age or name can influence some employers, although discrimination is not allowed by law.
The trial period and the contract type can be unclear if you do not read the contract carefully.

topics.context: Tell people you know that you are looking for work. Many vacancies are filled by word of mouth, and you can still apply on the portals and register at the IEFP at the same time.
phrases: Estou à procura de trabalho na restauração. (I'm looking for work in the restaurant trade.)
Envio-lhe o meu currículo em anexo. (I'm sending you my CV attached.)
Quanto tempo dura o período experimental? (How long is the trial period?)
O contrato é a termo ou sem termo? (Is the contract fixed-term or permanent?)
Trabalhei três anos numa loja. (I worked in a shop for three years.)
Se quiser, posso começar na segunda-feira. (If you like, I can start on Monday.)

sources.label: IEFP – Instituto do Emprego e Formação Profissional

quiz.prompt: What is a “cunha”?
options: A job obtained through a personal connection
quiz.answer: A job obtained through a personal connection
quiz.explain: The word is usually used critically, but asking people you know for tips is normal.

quiz.prompt: What is the período experimental?
options: A trial period at the start of a contract
quiz.answer: A trial period at the start of a contract
quiz.explain: During the trial period either side can end the contract more easily. Its length depends on the contract and the job.

quiz.prompt: Is a photo on the CV required in Portugal?
options: No, and it is never used
quiz.explain: Many CVs have a photo, but it is not required.

topics.title: Cars, trains and getting around
topics.intro: In Portugal, how you travel depends on where you live: in Lisbon and Porto many people use the metro, buses and suburban trains, and between cities the CP trains and long-distance coaches. In smaller places and in much of the interior, a car is often needed. For drivers, motorway tolls (portagens), speed limits and alcohol limits are part of daily life.
topics.question: Como é que te deslocas na tua cidade? (How do you get around in your town?)
facts: CP (Comboios de Portugal) runs the national trains: the Alfa Pendular and Intercidades between the main cities, and urban trains (comboios urbanos) around Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra. Lisbon and Porto each have a metro.
Many motorways have tolls (portagens). Some have toll booths, others only electronic tolls. Many drivers use a Via Verde device in the car, which pays automatically.
General speed limits for cars: 50 km/h in towns, 90 km/h on other roads, 100 km/h on roads reserved for motor vehicles and 120 km/h on motorways (auto-estradas). Signs can set lower limits.
The general blood alcohol limit for drivers is 0.5 g/l. For new drivers (in their first years) and professional drivers it is 0.2 g/l.

Cars must pass a periodic technical inspection (inspeção periódica obrigatória) at an inspection centre. A driving licence from another country: whether you can use it or must exchange it depends on the country; check with the IMT.

prosCons.prosLabel: Why many people use a car
pros: It is flexible for villages, shift work and trips with children.
Outside the big cities, buses and trains can be rare.
It saves time on routes without a direct train.
prosCons.consLabel: Why many people prefer public transport
cons: Tolls, fuel and parking in the city centres cost a lot.
In Lisbon and Porto, metro and trains are often faster at rush hour.
Monthly passes for public transport in the metropolitan areas can be cheaper than driving.

topics.context: If you plan to drive, check three things early: your licence (at the IMT), the insurance, and how you will pay electronic tolls. Ask at the IMT or look at imt-ip.pt.
phrases: Como é que chego à estação de comboios? (How do I get to the train station?)
Um bilhete de ida e volta para o Porto, se faz favor. (A return ticket to Porto, please.)
Onde é que posso estacionar por aqui? (Where can I park around here?)
Esta autoestrada tem portagens? (Does this motorway have tolls?)
Posso trocar a minha carta de condução? (Can I exchange my driving licence?)
Não bebi nada, vou conduzir. (I haven't drunk anything, I'm driving.)

sources.label: ANSR – Autoridade Nacional de Segurança Rodoviária

quiz.prompt: What is the general speed limit for cars on a Portuguese motorway?
quiz.explain: 120 km/h on auto-estradas, unless signs say otherwise.

quiz.prompt: What is Via Verde?
options: A device that pays motorway tolls automatically
quiz.answer: A device that pays motorway tolls automatically
quiz.explain: Many motorways have electronic tolls, and Via Verde pays them as you drive through.

quiz.prompt: Can you always use a foreign licence in Portugal?
options: It depends on the country of the licence
quiz.answer: It depends on the country of the licence
quiz.explain: Whether you can use it or must exchange it depends on the country. Check with the IMT.

topics.title: Women and men at work
topics.intro: In Portugal, many women work full time, and the law gives both parents rights to leave after a birth, with a period that only the father can take. A pay gap between women and men remains in the official statistics. Many people debate how large it is and how to close it.
topics.question: Como é que se dividem o trabalho e os cuidados no teu país? (How are work and care shared in your country?)
facts: After a birth, parents have the licença parental inicial (initial parental leave), which they can share between them. Part of the leave is reserved for the mother, and the father has his own leave that only he can take. The number of days and the payment rules have changed in recent years; check them with the Segurança Social.
The CITE (Comissão para a Igualdade no Trabalho e no Emprego) is the public body for equality at work and for the rights of working parents. You can ask it for information.
Portuguese names usually include surnames from both parents. A person who marries keeps their own surnames and may add the spouse's surname, but nobody has to.
Official statistics (INE, and the Gabinete de Estratégia e Planeamento of the Ministry of Labour) show that on average women earn less than men. The size of the gap depends on how it is measured.

Researchers point to several reasons, such as sector, occupation, years in the company and the fact that care for children and older relatives still falls more often on women. People disagree about the weight of each reason.

prosCons.prosLabel: What many people point to as progress
pros: A leave period reserved for fathers supports shared care.
Equal pay for equal work is in the law, and the CITE gives information.
Published statistics make the debate more factual.
prosCons.consLabel: What many people say is still open
cons: The gap in average earnings remains.
Care work still falls more often on women.
People disagree about the reasons and the best measures.

topics.context: If you have a question about leave or pay, ask the human resources department (recursos humanos), your union, the CITE or the Segurança Social. Do not rely only on a colleague's opinion.
phrases: Quero pedir a licença parental. (I want to apply for parental leave.)
O meu marido e eu dividimos as tarefas. (My husband and I share the tasks.)
Os meus apelidos são Costa e Silva. (My surnames are Costa and Silva.)
Quantas horas tem o horário a tempo parcial? (How many hours is the part-time schedule?)
Para trabalho igual, salário igual. (Equal pay for equal work.)

sources.label: CITE – Comissão para a Igualdade no Trabalho e no Emprego

quiz.prompt: What is true of parental leave after a birth?
options: Parents can share it, and part of it is only for the father
quiz.answer: Parents can share it, and part of it is only for the father
quiz.explain: The initial leave can be shared, and the father has his own leave that only he can take.

quiz.prompt: What is the CITE?
options: A public body for equality at work
quiz.answer: A public body for equality at work
quiz.explain: The CITE gives information on equality at work and on the rights of working parents.

quiz.prompt: A woman gets married. What happens to her surnames?
options: She must take her husband's surname
She keeps her own and may add her spouse's
quiz.answer: She keeps her own and may add her spouse's
quiz.explain: Adding the spouse's surname is a choice, not a duty.

topics.title: Dating basics
topics.intro: In Portugal, a first date often starts with combinar (to arrange to meet) and tomar um café or beber um copo (to have a coffee or a drink). Many adults meet through friends, work, hobbies or dating apps. Be clear, be respectful, and listen to the other person's answer.
topics.question: Como é que se marca um primeiro encontro no teu país? (How do people arrange a first date in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It varies by person, age, region and city.
“Combinar” means to arrange to meet. “Queres ir tomar um café?” is a relaxed first invitation; “beber um copo” is to have a drink.
Many adults use dating apps, but many also meet through friends, at work, in classes or in clubs.
Who pays varies. Some people split, some take turns, and sometimes one person pays the first time. Say what you prefer in a friendly way: “Pagamos a meias?”
Meeting the family usually comes later, when the relationship is clearer. “Não” or “Não me apetece” is a full answer, and it must be respected.
topics.context: Be honest and clear about what you want. If you do not want a second date, you can say it kindly: “Gostei muito, mas acho que não é o que procuro.”
phrases: Queres ir tomar um café amanhã? (Would you like to go for a coffee tomorrow?)
Gostei muito desta noite. (I really enjoyed this evening.)
Pagamos a meias? (Shall we split it?)
Prefiro ir com calma. (I prefer to take it slowly.)

topics.title: Direct and indirect
topics.intro: In Portugal, many people avoid a blunt “no”, especially with people they do not know well. A “pois” can mean yes, I see, or a polite doubt, and “logo se vê” often means no decision yet. Learning to hear these soft answers, and to ask kindly for a clear one, makes life much easier.
topics.question: Como é que dizes que não sem ofender? (How do you say no without offending?)

table.label: What is said, and what it can mean
rows: Pois.
Yes, right, I see, or a polite doubt. The tone shows which one. “Pois é” usually agrees.
Logo se vê.
We'll see. Often no decision yet, sometimes a soft no.
Temos de combinar qualquer coisa.
A friendly wish to meet, without a fixed plan. Suggest a day if you want to meet.
Vou ver o que posso fazer.
Maybe. It can be a real effort or a polite way to lower your hopes.
Não se preocupe.
It's fine, or please don't worry. The tone shows which one.
Se calhar…
Perhaps… Often softens a suggestion or a disagreement: “Se calhar é melhor esperar.”

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the region, the age and the relationship.
Disagreement is often softened: “Se calhar…”, “Não sei se…”, “Acho que não é bem assim”. This is politeness, not uncertainty.
In offices, a soft answer can hide a clear rule. If you hear “Isso agora é complicado”, ask directly what is missing: “O que é que falta?”
In shops and cafés, a plain “Não, obrigado” or “Não, obrigada” is normal and polite. You do not need an excuse.
If you are not sure what an answer means, repeat it in your own words: “Então, fica combinado para quinta-feira?”
topics.context: Style varies a lot by region and person. A friendly question for a concrete answer (a day, a document, a yes or a no) is clearer for both sides and is not rude.
phrases: Pois, tem razão. (Right, you have a point.)
Logo se vê. (We'll see.)
Se calhar é melhor esperar. (Perhaps it's better to wait.)
Vou ver o que posso fazer. (I'll see what I can do.)
Então, fica combinado para quinta? (So, is it agreed for Thursday?)
Não, obrigada, estou servida. (No, thank you, I've had enough. Said by a woman.)

quiz.explain: Logo se vê means we'll see. Ask again later, or suggest a day.

quiz.explain: Pois is very common and depends on the tone. Pois é usually agrees.

quiz.explain: “O que é que falta?” turns a soft answer into a concrete next step.

topics.title: Humour and banter
topics.intro: In Portugal, many people use humour to build closeness: gozar (to tease), irony and self-irony about bureaucracy, the weather or football are common among friends and colleagues. Friendly rivalry between Lisbon and Porto is a classic topic, so listen first and join in when you know the people. Some carnivals, such as the one in Torres Vedras, are known for satirical floats about current events.
topics.question: Com quem é que brincas e com quem não? (Who do you joke with and who not?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the situation.
“Gozar com alguém” means to tease or make fun of someone. “Estás a gozar?” means “Are you kidding?”, and “Estou a brincar” means “I'm only joking”.
Irony is common: someone may say “Que maravilha!” when something goes wrong. Tone and face show it.
Jokes about regions are often heard, for example the nicknames alfacinhas for people from Lisbon and tripeiros for people from Porto. They are usually friendly, but if you are new, do not start them.
Self-irony about queues, paperwork and slow replies is common. Many people laugh about the system, but that does not mean they want an outsider to criticise it.

pros: Teasing between friends is a sign of trust.
Irony makes difficult things easier to say.
Satire at carnival and in the media is a long tradition.
cons: A joke that works in one group may hurt in another.
As a newcomer, you may not know the limits yet.
Jokes about origin, religion or looks can hurt, even if the speaker means well.

topics.context: Join the banter with a small, kind joke about yourself first, such as your own mistakes in Portuguese. If someone looks upset, say “Estava a brincar, desculpa”.
phrases: Estás a gozar comigo? (Are you kidding me?)
Estava a brincar, desculpa. (I was only joking, sorry.)
Que maravilha… (Wonderful… Said ironically.)
Essa foi boa! (That was a good one!)
Essa piada não tem graça para mim. (That joke isn't funny to me.)
O meu português é uma desgraça, mas eu tento. (My Portuguese is a disaster, but I'm trying.)

quiz.prompt: What does “Estás a gozar?” mean?
quiz.explain: Gozar com alguém is to tease someone. “Estou a brincar” says it was not serious.

quiz.explain: Regional jokes are common, but they depend on the group.
